title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash
gist: Meta removed the word 'train' from commercial terms taking effect October 30 after publisher backlash, but legal experts say the language still allows scraping of business-page websites to develop AI-linked 'business products'. News groups in the UK, EU and US are urging regulators to block the terms.

insights.claim: Meta deleted 'train' and 'any content' from its commercial terms but still lets it pull updates from business users' websites to 'provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products'.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The substantive scraping right survives the edit, so AI-use risk for publishers is rhetorically reduced but not legally removed.

insights.claim: Legal experts argue 'develop' is broad enough to include training, and 'business product' is undefined, so dropping the word 'train' changes little.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Ambiguous contract terms are where later AI-training claims get litigated, which raises legal risk for Meta.
insights.quote: “That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.’”

insights.claim: Meta did not notify users of the changed wording and its statement addressed the first Nieman Lab report but not the follow-up, which may add confusion ahead of the rollout.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Quiet edits invite regulatory scrutiny and weaken the credibility of Meta's reassurances.

insights.claim: Because honoring robots.txt is voluntary, and the enforceable terms of service do not mention it, Meta could in principle scrape sites that block crawlers; only a contractual commitment would make publisher preferences binding.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Publishers' main technical opt-out has no legal force against a platform whose contract overrides it, so licensing leverage rests on contract language.
insights.quote: “you can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,”

insights.claim: Meta says the consolidated crawling terms apply only to its ads and business products and that content owners can still use robots.txt, and that it is not about scraping news sites.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: This is the company's stated position and sets a standard it can be held to if enforcement is attempted.

insights.claim: Publisher groups in the UK, EU and US each asked regulators to intervene, with the News/Media Alliance calling the policy an abuse of market power because Meta conditions audience access on content scraping.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Framing the terms as tying access to data creates a competition-law angle, not just a copyright one.
insights.quote: “It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30,”

insights.claim: The dispute positions platform terms as a way to avoid per-publisher AI licensing fees, since experts say Meta could sidestep millions in news licensing by requiring business users to share data as a condition of having a page.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: If it holds, platform terms become a cheaper route to training data than licensing deals, pressuring the AI content-licensing market.
